column1: What combinatorial problem does Kafka's log-based architecture solve, and what is the complexity reduction?
column2: It solves the point-to-point integration explosion of O(N×M) producers-to-consumers by inserting a durable, replayable log as universal integration layer, reducing complexity to O(N+M).

column1: What three invariant properties define a Kafka commit log?
column2: 1) Append-only (no in-place mutation), 2) Ordered (monotonically increasing offset per partition), 3) Durable by definition (write acknowledged only after persistence/replication).

column1: Within what scope does Kafka guarantee message ordering, and why doesn't it guarantee global ordering?
column2: Ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition (by offset). Global ordering across partitions is not guaranteed because that would require a single-threaded serial log, sacrificing scalability.

column1: What are the three distinct offset values associated with every Kafka message, and who assigns/controls each?
column2: 1) Log offset — immutable position assigned by the broker on write. 2) Consumer offset — last offset committed by a consumer group. 3) High-water mark — highest offset replicated to all ISRs, assigned by the leader; determines read visibility.

column1: Why can't consumers read beyond the high-water mark in a Kafka partition?
column2: Because the high-water mark marks the highest offset replicated to all in-sync replicas; reading beyond it risks exposing data that could be lost if the leader fails before replication completes.

column1: What is the mathematical relationship between partition count and consumer parallelism in a Kafka consumer group?
column2: Each partition can be consumed by exactly one consumer within a group, so max-parallelism = partition-count. Throughput = partitions × per-partition-throughput.

column1: What mechanism allows Kafka to serve consumer fetch requests with zero-copy transfer, and what overhead does it eliminate?
column2: The sendfile(2) syscall (Java FileChannel.transferTo()) transfers data directly from OS page cache to network socket, eliminating 2 memory copies and 2 context switches per message batch (bypassing user space entirely).

column1: Why does Kafka deliberately avoid maintaining its own application-level cache?
column2: It delegates caching to the OS page cache, allowing the JVM heap to stay small (reducing GC pressure) while the OS manages much larger amounts of cached log data more efficiently; data also survives process restarts.

column1: What does acks=all guarantee, and what is a common misconception about this setting?
column2: acks=all means the leader waits for acknowledgment from all In-Sync Replicas (ISR) before confirming the write to the producer, providing the strongest durability. Misconception: this is NOT synchronous two-phase commit — the leader doesn't block followers; it tracks the high-watermark asynchronously.

column1: What two settings constitute the conventional balance between durability and availability in Kafka replication, and what failure do they tolerate?
column2: Replication factor of 3 with min.insync.replicas=2 tolerates one broker failure without data loss while bounding replication fan-out/throughput cost.

column1: What are the two requirements to enable exactly-once semantics (EOS) in Kafka, beyond the default at-least-once delivery?
column2: 1) Idempotent producers (enable.idempotence=true) to prevent duplicate writes on retry. 2) For cross-partition/topic operations, transactional semantics (transactional producer API) to atomically commit across partitions.

column1: What two distinct integrity mechanisms does Kafka use, and what attack surface does each protect against?
column2: CRC32C checksum (per record batch) protects against storage-layer bit rot and broker-side corruption. TLS (AEAD ciphers) protects against network interception/tampering. Neither substitutes for application-level content validation.
